title: Iran Closes Strait of Hormuz Cutting Ship Traffic from 130 to Under 10 Per Day
description_short: Iran’s reported control of the Strait of Hormuz is linked to conflicting traffic figures and an unverified ceasefire memorandum.

description_long: A New York Times investigation published in December 2025 examined cryptocurrency enforcement cases that were active when Donald Trump returned to office. According to the supplied account, the SEC had eased up on more than 60% of those matters, through dismissals, pauses or other changes. Examples included the agency’s case against Coinbase, which accused the exchange of operating as an unregistered securities broker, and enforcement actions involving Ripple, Kraken, Gemini, Binance and Robinhood. The account also says a case involving Justin Sun was paused after his investment in World Liberty Financial and later settled for $10 million without an admission of wrongdoing. title: Federal Judge Blocks Most of Trump’s Election Order, Including Proof-of-Citizenship Rules
description_short: A federal court blocked most of Trump’s election order, including its proof-of-citizenship voter-registration rule.
description_medium: Trump’s March 2025 election order sought to require documentary proof of citizenship for voter registration, restrict counting of mail ballots that arrived after Election Day and withhold some federal funds from states that did not comply. In June 2026, a federal judge permanently barred most of the order, ruling that the president lacks specific constitutional authority over election procedures.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed an election executive order in March 2025 that sought to change voter-registration and ballot-counting rules. Among its provisions were documentary proof of citizenship for registration, limits on counting mail ballots arriving after Election Day even when they were postmarked on time, and potential loss of federal funds for states that did not comply. A federal judge in Massachusetts later permanently barred most of the order. The court rejected the administration’s argument that the lawsuit was premature and concluded that the Constitution assigns election regulation to Congress and the states, not the president. The ruling converted an earlier preliminary injunction into a permanent one. The case therefore documents both an executive attempt to set national election requirements and a judicial limit on that authority. The supplied source does not substantiate every additional claim in the original description about machine decertification or access to voter files, so those details are omitted.
organization_tags: U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts
notes: The linked PBS/AP report supports the proof-of-citizenship rule, mail-ballot provision, funding threat and permanent injunction. The revised title and text omit unsupported claims about machine decertification and DOGE access to voter files.
